chapter: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
title: Blanton's harmonic sophistication and Ellington's writing for bass
summary: They discuss Blanton's notes forming independent melodies in Ellington's writing; the two seldom talked bass but admired each other's style.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Well, did you -- did you talk much with Blanton? Did you and Blanton talk about bass, playing the bass much?
Well, did you -- did you find him very sophisticated harmonically?
Oh, yes. Yes. He played wonderful notes on the bass where they would fit in very well with the chorus and what have you.
Yeah, because he was, because the things he was playing weren't, he was playing more than just the fundamental --
Yeah, but then too some of the things I noticed, like that -- that was something I wanted to ask about, you about, too, about like the writing for the bass because one
of the things that I noticed in Duke Ellington's writing for the bass is that oftentimes the harmony part that the bass plays is also an independent melody.

You know, and it's not at times, like you listen to 'Concerto for Cootie' or something, the notes that Jimmy Blanton was playing, even though they fit the chords. And you subtracted that, you removed everything else from the arrangement, those notes themselves would be a melody.
Do you -- and he also played like that too.
What's it like -- well, like that is did you ever discuss with him any of those kinds of ideas about playing the bass?
Well, no, not really. I didn't see him quite that much, you know. So we never did -- we never did hardly talk any bass, you know. We praised each other.
He liked the way I -- my style, and I loved his, you know.
